label: Geometric and Analytic Consequences of CD(K,N)
notes: This chapter, printed pages 847 through 902, harvests the payoff of the synthetic curvature-dimension condition. From the single hypothesis CD(K,N) we derive a whole family of classical theorems: volume comparison, a finite diameter, Brunn-Minkowski, Poincare and log-Sobolev inequalities, and a spectral gap, all without any smooth Ricci tensor.

label: The CD(K,N) Hypothesis Recalled
notes: We restate the working hypothesis. A metric measure space satisfies CD(K,N) when the Renyi-type entropy is displacement convex along Wasserstein geodesics, with a distortion correction governed by K and N. This single convexity inequality is the engine that drives every consequence developed in the rest of the chapter.

label: From Convexity to Comparison
notes: The common move is always the same. Take two endpoint measures, run the Wasserstein geodesic between them, and read off the entropy convexity inequality. Specializing the endpoints to delta masses, balls, or uniform densities converts an abstract convexity statement into a sharp geometric or analytic comparison theorem.

label: Bishop-Gromov Volume Comparison
notes: Choosing a point mass and a uniform ball as endpoints turns displacement convexity into control of how volume grows with radius. The synthetic Bishop-Gromov theorem says the ratio of measured ball volume to the model-space comparison volume is nonincreasing in radius, exactly as in the smooth Riemannian setting.

label: Bonnet-Myers Diameter Bound
notes: When K is strictly positive, Bishop-Gromov volume control forces space to close up. The synthetic Bonnet-Myers theorem caps the diameter by pi times the square root of N minus one over K. Positive curvature plus finite dimension means the space cannot be larger than the comparison sphere.

label: The Brunn-Minkowski Inequality
notes: Interpolating between two sets by transporting one onto the other yields a synthetic Brunn-Minkowski inequality. The measure of the midpoint set dominates a distortion-weighted mean of the endpoint measures. Flat space recovers the classical inequality, while positive curvature improves it through the comparison coefficients.

label: The Poincare Inequality
notes: With K positive the entropy is uniformly convex, and linearizing that convexity around the uniform measure produces a spectral-gap Poincare inequality. The variance of any function is bounded by a curvature-dimension constant times the Dirichlet energy, controlling fluctuations of every observable on the space.

label: The Logarithmic Sobolev Inequality
notes: Uniform displacement convexity of entropy is exactly the hypothesis that yields a logarithmic Sobolev inequality. Relative entropy is bounded by the Fisher information divided by twice the curvature constant. This sharpens Poincare, governs exponential convergence of the heat semigroup, and encodes Gaussian-type concentration of measure.

label: Lichnerowicz Spectral Gap
notes: Translating the Poincare constant into the language of the Laplacian gives the Lichnerowicz bound. The first nonzero eigenvalue is at least K times N over N minus one. On the round sphere this is sharp, with equality realized by the first spherical harmonics, anchoring the synthetic estimate to a classical model.

label: One Hypothesis, Many Theorems
notes: This is the organizing picture. The single node CD(K,N) fans out into volume comparison, a diameter cap, Brunn-Minkowski, the Poincare and log-Sobolev inequalities, and the spectral gap. Every arrow is a specialization of the same entropy convexity along Wasserstein geodesics, the unifying mechanism of the theory.

label: Stability and Local-to-Global
notes: These consequences survive measured Gromov-Hausdorff limits, since displacement convexity is stable under such convergence. The local-to-global property shows a uniform local curvature bound upgrades to a global one. Thus the synthetic framework is closed: limits of CD(K,N) spaces remain CD(K,N) and keep every theorem.

label: Synthesis and Outlook
notes: We close by collecting the dictionary. One synthetic hypothesis reproduces the geometric and analytic core of Ricci-bounded geometry without derivatives, extends it to singular spaces, and stays stable under limits. The open frontier is rigidity and the Riemannian curvature-dimension refinement that pins down when equality holds.
